A study of insane female offenders found the Pearson correlation between total PCL-R score and IQ was r = -0.55, meaning higher psychopathy predicted lower cognitive performance.

Research on callous-unemotional traits and amygdala dysfunction links reduced fear conditioning and emotional processing to impaired aversive learning, which weakens the emotional inhibition that would otherwise deter repeated offending.
Radford University’s serial killer IQ data show the average serial killer IQ is 95.1, with the sample of 202 serial killers clustering around normal rather than exceptional intelligence.
The empirical data contradict the assumption that serial homicide offenders systematically have superior IQ; Radford’s sample mean is 95.1, below the population mean of 100.

Neuroimaging and neuropsychological studies link psychopathy to impaired ventromedial/orbitofrontal prefrontal cortex function, with social-affective decision making and reinforcement-based learning appearing disrupted while some executive functions can remain relatively intact.

FBI homicide clearance data show that only 54% of homicides were cleared in 2020, meaning 46% remained unsolved, and reported clearance for 2024 was 61%. (54% clearance rate in 2020 vs 61% reported for 2024)

The peer-reviewed literature reports a consistent association between psychopathy and reduced prefrontal gray matter, especially in vmPFC/OFC and anterior cingulate cortex, but the causal interpretation remains contested because studies also propose broader limbic and fronto-limbic connectivity explanations rather than a single prefrontal deficit.

Controlled studies of high-psychopathy participants have found that they can perform normally on some attentional and cognitive tasks despite showing characteristic emotional and behavioral abnormalities.

Researchers using the Radford University Serial Killer Database note that it is a secondary-source database relying on self-reports and third-party reports, so cognitive assessments and other offender data may be incomplete or affected by memory errors, exaggeration, and misinformation.
The Radford Serial Killer Database reports IQ information for 202 serial killers, and those offenders appear to be of normal IQ overall (median 89.0, mean 95.1), with scores ranging from 57 to 165.
A meta-analytic review found a small, statistically significant negative relationship between intelligence and psychopathy, with total psychopathy correlated with FSIQ at r = -.07.

Neuropsychological and neuroimaging studies have linked psychopathy to executive and prefrontal deficits, often using psychopathy measures such as the PCL-R alongside tasks and brain imaging to assess executive function and prefrontal cortex activity.

FBI guidance on serial homicide emphasizes that offenders can operate for long periods without detection, and serial homicide is often harder to identify and clear than single-incident homicide because cases are dispersed across time and jurisdictions.

Research on callous-unemotional traits and amygdala dysfunction indicates that reduced emotional responsiveness and impaired threat/fear processing are associated with psychopathic traits and may help explain repeated violent offending.

The best-known database evidence does not support the stereotype of an exceptionally intelligent serial killer: the Radford Serial Killer IQ sample had a mean IQ of 95.1 and median of 89.0, which is around average to slightly below average.

The peer-reviewed literature still debates whether observed psychopathy-related brain differences are causes, consequences, or correlates of violent behavior, and whether structural versus functional prefrontal/amygdala findings reflect developmental deficits, environmental effects, or sample-specific criminal history.

Available data sources do not support the assumption that serial homicide offenders are typically highly intelligent and especially hard to apprehend; the Radford serial killer IQ dataset instead shows an average profile near the general population norm.

A 2019 meta-analysis of 29 unique homicide offender samples from 22 studies (2,603 offenders) found the mean PCL-R score for homicide offenders was 21.2, and that serial homicide showed a larger association (r = 0.74) than homicide overall.

In a preliminary neuropsychological study of homicide offenders, cluster analysis identified one subgroup with low psychopathy and high psychosis and another with high psychopathy and low psychosis, each showing distinct differences in intelligence, memory, attention, executive functions, and academic abilities.
A 2019 review found the overall psychopathy–homicide association was large (r = 0.68), and it was stronger in serial homicide (r = 0.74) than in homicide overall.

A 2019 study of young violent offenders found that intelligence was not necessarily pertinent to understanding aggressive antisocial or psychopathic behaviors, and that the interpersonal and affective psychopathy facets had very low impact on explained variance in aggressive antisocial behavior.
A nationwide study reported that homicidal adolescents with psychopathy-like personality characteristics formed a special subgroup among other homicidal youngsters.
A 2023 condemned-capital-murderer sample found that one-third of individuals were clinically psychopathic with PCL-R scores of 30 or greater, and the sample mean score was 23.31.

The psychopathy–homicide link is clearly supported at the group level, but the 2019 meta-analysis also showed it is strongest in more severe forms of homicide such as serial homicide (r = 0.74) and multi-offender homicide (r = 0.80), making the size of the association a debated point across homicide subtypes.
